To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the genetic makeup (i.e., single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)) of individuals plays a critical role in the pathophysiology of asthma.

we have shown that the genetic variants associated with asthma and/or related phenotypes in several genes have functional consequences, and that these variants are likely to play a role in asthma pathophysiology.
genetic variability in asthma is a major determinant of treatment response and that the mechanisms of asthma are complex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic basis of asthma, the identification of genetic markers for asthma susceptibility and severity, and the development of new therapeutic approaches for asthma.
the identification of genetic variants associated with asthma and the elucidation of the mechanisms by which these variants influence asthma susceptibility and/or severity.
understanding the molecular mechanisms by which genetic variants affect asthma pathophysiology and treatment responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we still know very little about the genetic determinants of asthma.
we are not quite there yet, but we are getting closer.
the genetic determinants of asthma are still largely uncharacterized and the functional mechanisms remain to be elucidated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic determinants of asthma are not only relevant but also have important implications in the pathophysiology of the disease.
the functional impacts of asthma-related genetic variants are diverse and complex.

the genetic determinants of asthma are relevant and have implications for asthma pathophysiology, and that further investigations are needed to understand the mechanisms by which these determinants contribute to the disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the field of genetic research in asthma is moving forward and that the functional characterization of disease-associated SNPS will continue to be a major focus.
genetic variability can be used to identify individuals at risk, and to predict treatment response.
the genetic makeup in the promoter and 3′ untranslated region of a gene can have profound impact on the gene expression level and thus the protein levels in the cell.
